analysis.one_liner: Bans banks and financial firms from financing new fossil fuel production.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Bank Holding Company Act to bar banks, bank holding companies, insured depository institutions, and their affiliates from lending to, investing in, or otherwise financing fossil fuel production from new sources or new fossil infrastructure like pipelines, wells, and refineries. It also bans securitizing or trading derivatives tied to new fossil fuel production. Violations would carry criminal penalties of up to five years and fines of up to $5 million per day, plus civil penalties, forfeiture of violation-related revenue, and bans from future work at banks or public companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people on the exposure side of climate and financial risk: the bill's premise is that unrestricted lending to expand fossil fuel production builds a 'carbon bubble' — assets that could lose value abruptly if climate policy or markets shift — and that cutting off new financing protects the economy, bank depositors, and taxpayers who would otherwise backstop failing banks. Communities near new extraction and pipeline projects would also see less new construction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors, taxpayers, and communities facing climate and financial risk

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits financial companies from providing loans or investments to fossil fuel companies and projects, and from facilitating transactions, securitizing assets, or entering derivatives that fund new fossil fuel production [S2][S3]

Backs the ban with criminal penalties up to 5 years imprisonment and fines up to $5 million per day for willful violations, forfeiture of violation revenues, civil penalties, and lifetime bans from banking or public-company employment for individual violators [S3]
Requires each covered company to maintain compliance policies and requires its chief executive to attest to compliance under regulator supervision [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large banks and other financial firms would lose a major line of lending and fee business, and fossil fuel companies would lose access to the bank financing they need to open new wells, mines, pipelines, and terminals. If financing dried up faster than demand fell, energy prices could rise for consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks and fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: The financing ban is written broadly: it covers not just new extraction but financial activity with fossil fuel companies and projects generally, which could restrict ordinary commercial banking relationships across the energy sector [S3]

Cutting off credit for new fossil production could raise energy costs for consumers before clean alternatives are fully built out, and enforcement based on per-day criminal fines against institutions raises hard questions about how liability would fall on individual employees [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at a real, large-scale risk — financial system exposure to fossil fuel assets that could become worthless — and paired it with unusually stiff enforcement. But its breadth (covering general financial relationships with fossil fuel companies, not only new production) and its one-sponsor origin with no cosponsors meant it was never tested in committee, never amended, and never debated, so whether the costs to consumers and the banking system would have outweighed the climate and financial-stability gains was never examined on the record.

outcome.mechanism: Merkley introduced it on October 21, 2020, and it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on October 21, 2020 [S1][S5]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, which took no further action on it [S5]
No senator joined as a cosponsor; the bill shows zero cosponsors for the entire Congress [S4]
The bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without ever reaching the Senate floor [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and fossil fuel producers, who kept unrestricted access to the financing channels the bill would have closed — no hearing or vote ever tested the restriction. The status quo of bank lending to expand fossil fuel production continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big banks and fossil fuel producers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it received no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote or cosponsor ever came from either party; the bill's only recorded support was its Democratic sponsor, with zero cosponsors of any party [S4].

industries.note: They would lose lending, investment, underwriting, securitization, and derivatives business tied to fossil fuel companies and new fossil projects, with criminal and civil penalties for violations [S2][S3]. Their interest in keeping that revenue open ran against the bill's aim of cutting off new fossil fuel financing [S3].

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers (oil, gas, and coal)
industries.note: They would lose a primary source of capital for new wells, mines, pipelines, terminals, and refineries [S2][S3]. The bill treated expanded production as a driver of climate and financial risk that ordinary people bear [S3].

The ban on securitizing assets that fund new fossil production and on related derivatives would remove fossil-linked paper from markets, reducing both trading profits and the exposure of pension and retirement portfolios to a potential 'carbon bubble' [S2][S3].
